edges.description: The breached epidermis allows S. aureus, S. pyogenes, or both to establish and proliferate locally.
S. pyogenes, S. aureus, or both proliferate locally to produce vesiculopustules and crusted erosions.
Toxigenic S. aureus expresses exfoliative toxins at the infected epidermal site.
edges.target: Exfoliative Toxin Production by S. aureus

edges.description: Superficial pyogenic infection produces vesicles from the initial erythematous papules.
Neutrophil-rich superficial infection produces thin-walled pustules.
Vesicles and pustules rupture and dry into the characteristic crusted superficial erosions.
Group A streptococcal skin infection can antecede acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and acute rheumatic fever in endemic communities.
Secreted exfoliative toxin reaches superficial keratinocyte desmosomes and cleaves desmoglein 1.
edges.source: Exfoliative Toxin Production by S. aureus

edges.description: Loss of the adhesive Dsg1 ectodomain is sufficient to produce the superficial intraepidermal blister.
The superficial intraepidermal split manifests clinically as flaccid bullae in bullous impetigo.
The fragile bullae rupture into moist erosions that crust over.
Scabies-associated pruritus and scratching damage the epidermis, opening the barrier breaks in which impetigo arises.
Crowding raises the chance that S. aureus or S. pyogenes reaches and colonizes breached skin.
Poor hygiene favors transfer and persistence of the causative bacteria on the skin.
Hot, humid climates predispose to impetigo; the intermediate steps are not specified by the source.

nodes.description: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins are glutamate-specific serine proteases that cleave one peptide bond in the extracellular region of desmoglein 1, disrupting superficial keratinocyte adhesion at desmosomes.

evidence.reference_title: Staphylococcal exfoliative toxins: "molecular scissors" of bacteria that attack the cutaneous defense barrier in mammals.
evidence.snippet: the three isoforms of ETs, i.e., ETA, ETB, and ETD, are glutamate-specific serine proteases that specifically and efficiently cleave a single peptide bond in the extracellular region of human and mouse desmoglein 1 (Dsg1), a desmosomal intercellular adhesion molecule

evidence.reference_title: Removal of amino-terminal extracellular domains of desmoglein 1 by staphylococcal exfoliative toxin is sufficient to initiate epidermal blister formation.
evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that the removal of amino-terminal extracellular domains of Dsg1 by ETs is sufficient to initiate epidermal blister formation in bullous impetigo and SSSS.

nodes.description: Limited impetigo is treated with topical antibiotics such as mupirocin, retapamulin, ozenoxacin, or fusidic acid, which kill S. aureus and S. pyogenes locally and shorten the contagious superficial infection. Resistance limits these agents: the fusidic acid-resistant epidemic European impetigo clone (EEFIC) of S. aureus has persisted in Belgium, and a variant of it carrying mupirocin resistance has spread among children there.

evidence.snippet: Topical mupirocin 2% ointment or retapamulin 1% ointment are the recommended initial treatments for mild, nonbullous and bullous impetigo.

evidence.reference_title: Interventions for impetigo.
evidence.snippet: Topical antibiotics showed better cure rates than placebo (pooled odds ratio (OR) 6.49, 95% confidence interval (CI) 3.93 to 10.73)

evidence.reference_title: Interventions for impetigo.
evidence.snippet: There is good evidence that topical mupirocin and topical fusidic acid are equally, or more effective than oral treatment for people with limited disease.

evidence.snippet: EEFIC isolates were mostly isolated from young patients with impetigo and showed a seasonal late summer peak.

evidence.snippet: We highlight the spread of a mupirocin-resistant EEFIC in children, with a seasonal trend for the third quarter of the year. This is of concern because this variant is resistant to the two main topical antibiotics used to treat impetigo in Belgium.
